Today I learned that the first safety control in a nuclear reactor against meltdown was a man weilding an axe.

From the article:

The Chicago plant is notable for being the first to reach a state in which its nuclear-fission chain reaction was self-sustaining. Despite that achievement, however, emergency precautions at the time weren't very high-tech, at least by today’s standards. Those precautions included workers suspending a thin rod of cadmium from a rope so that it dangled above a hole in the reactor. They used cadmium because it can slow down or stop a nuclear reaction by absorbing neutrons, hopefully stemming a disaster. But there was no automatic mechanism to make the cadmium fall into the hole. Instead, a museum sign explains, a “sturdy young male physicist stood by the rope, holding an axe.” (You can’t make this stuff up.) If something went wrong, he’d “swing his axe and cut the rope, plunging the rod into its hole and shutting down the reaction instantly.” That earned him the name “Safety Control Rod Axe Man,” now SCRAM for short.

Yes it is, and for greater certainty - yes, it is worth going to college for a career in photography.

The photography program I took dealt with far more than the simple mechanics of the camera and light. We covered

  • how the camera works and the relationship between shutter speed, aperture size, sensor capability, ISO, available light, and types of light,
  • the history of photography,
  • historical photographers and why their work is important,
  • the various aspects of composition,
  • colour theory,
  • printing, and (to name but a few)
  • image editing, and related ethics.

All covered by professionals in their fields, and all of which you will find valuable unless you're more interested in snapshots than photographs.

Sure, you can go out buy a decent digital camera and some hopefully decent glass to go with it and start taking pictures. You can hope that you luck out and get what you need but if you're interested in a word of advice that's a coin flip with a 5 sided coin from the Alpha Omega quadrant - your odds are considerably less than 50/50.... then again you can get some really decent shots with a crop sensor and kit lens, provided you know how to work the camera and have a solid understanding of the capabilities/limitations of your hardware.

You could hope that whoever is behind the counter at the camera store is interested in talking to you about the fundamental differences between a full frame camera and an APS-C cropped sensor as it pertains to the genre of photography you are potentially interested in pursuing - and by "interested in talking to you" I mean having a greater interest in providing you with information about light, noise, and field of view than in simply selling you something on that particular day.

You can hope that s/he can, and will, tell you about the different types of lenses that could be used in your chosen genre of photography and whether you need fast glass, or can get good shots with a more economical lens. Whether you should be looking at a short telephoto, a longer telephoto, or a fast-ish prime lens...... and what that decision means for you the person holding the camera.

My advice is to take at least the basics. You don't necessarily have to take full program (if you're not interested in studio work the studio lighting component of a given program will not be relevant) but the basics of your camera and how it works with different lenses and light, composition, and historical perspective, are too important to leave up to "I'll eventually figure it out"

I've got some nice gear in my camera bag that I bought at really reasonable prices from people who thought that all they needed to become the next Adams, Capa, Cartier-Bresson, or Testino was a camera and a couple of lenses. People who ultimately ended up disillusioned, disappointed, and selling their hardware because their images were not coming out like they wanted them to because they didn't have the background knowledge to make that happen.

Good luck with whatever you decide to do, the world can always use another photographer and I hope we see some of your work here.
